# Priors {.unnumbered} *Roughly 30 minutes. Part B is arithmetic a child could do and most doctors cannot. Do it before you read Part C.* ## Part A: the assay You want to say "there is a 95% probability the true mean is in my interval". To be entitled to it you need one ingredient you did not have. The cleanest way to see what has nothing to do with beans; it is an eDNA survey. You are surveying ponds for a rare protected species. The assay is good: **sensitivity 90%** (if the species is there, you detect it nine times in ten) and a **false positive rate of 5%** (if it is absent, you get a spurious positive one time in twenty). You sample a pond. **It tests positive.** **What is the probability the species is there?** Commit before you scroll, nearest whole per cent. % ## Part B: the count Most people say something in the eighties or nineties. Here is the arithmetic, and the only trick is that we count ponds rather than juggle percentages. `edna_table()` is in `R/beans.R`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} edna_table() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|truth | n_ponds| test_positive| test_negative| |:---------------|-------:|-------------:|-------------:| |Species present | 20| 18| 2| |Species absent | 980| 49| 931|
::: ::: Read it aloud: - Of **1000** ponds, **20** hold the species. It is rare; that is why it is protected. - Of those 20, the assay detects **18**. - Of the **980** without it, **49** test positive anyway. - Positives total **18 + 49 = 67**. Of those, **18** truly have the species. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} prob_present_given_positive(prevalence = 0.02) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.2686567 ``` ::: ::: **About 27%.** A 90% sensitive assay, a 5% false positive rate, a positive in hand, and it is still more likely than not that the pond is empty. The reason is the 980: the species is so rare that a 5% error on the empties produces more false positives than there are true ones to find. :::{.callout-note} ## Why counts, not the formula This is not a teaching indulgence; it measurably works better. McDowell and Jacobs [@mcdowell2017] meta-analysed the literature: roughly **4%** solve problems of this shape when the information arrives as conditional probabilities, against roughly **24%** as natural frequencies. Read that honestly, though: 24% is a sixfold improvement on a catastrophic baseline and still means three-quarters get it wrong. The format helps; it does not do the thinking. The companion finding from Gigerenzer and Hoffrage [@gigerenzer1995] is the one to remember: 24 experienced physicians, given a prevalence, a sensitivity and a false positive rate, produced answers from **1% to 99%**. ::: ## Part C: change one thing Same assay, same positive result, but now the pond is in known good habitat where roughly half of ponds are occupied. **Before you run it, the answer will:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} edna_table(prevalence = 0.50) prob_present_given_positive(prevalence = 0.50) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|truth | n_ponds| test_positive| test_negative| |:---------------|-------:|-------------:|-------------:| |Species present | 500| 450| 50| |Species absent | 500| 25| 475|
::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.9473684 ``` ::: ::: **About 95%.** :::{.callout-important} ## Stop here Same assay. Same result. **27% against 95%.** The data did not change. What changed is what you believed **before** the measurement. That is a **prior**, and it is not decoration you can decline. In the first case it was doing 68 percentage points of work. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(prior = seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 500)) |> mutate(posterior = prob_present_given_positive(prior)) |> ggplot(aes(prior, posterior)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, colour = colorspace::qualitative_hcl(1, palette = "Dark 3")) + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, 1)) + labs(x = "Prior probability the species is present", y = "Posterior, given a positive test") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Posterior probability the species is present, given one positive test, against the prior. Assay characteristics identical throughout. The dashed line marks where a positive leaves the question even.](04-priors_files/figure-html/fig-prior-curve-1.png){#fig-prior-curve fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: One curve, one assay, every answer from near zero to near one. Pick your prior and read off your conclusion. ## Part D: the vocabulary, arrived at - **Prior:** what you believed before the data. Here, the prevalence. - **Likelihood:** what the data do. Here, the assay characteristics. - **Posterior:** what you believe after; the prior updated by the data. And a second definition of probability, incompatible with the long-run frequency you confirmed with the coin: a **degree of belief**, which can attach to a hypothesis or a parameter. Which is exactly what you wanted for your interval. :::{.callout-warning} ## The inversion, three times - **eDNA:** P(positive | present) is not P(present | positive). 90% against 27%. - **Your interval:** P(interval like mine | true mean X) is not P(true mean X | my interval). - **Next week:** P(data like mine | null true) is not P(null true | my data). That is the p-value, the same error a third time. One inversion, three costumes. If you have it here, you have all three. ::: ## Part E: so why not be Bayesian? Look at @fig-prior-curve again. The prior did 68 points of work. In the eDNA case that is fine: prevalence is measurable, so the prior *is* data. But if nobody has surveyed the ponds, you need a prior anyway, so you invent one, and your posterior is now partly invented in a proportion nobody can see. That is the frequentist objection, and it is not foolish: > Refuse to supply a prior. Say only what the data support. The price is that you can never make the statement you actually want, and you will spend your career correcting people who think you have. Pay it. :::{.callout-important} ## Where this module goes We do frequentist statistics for the next ten weeks. Not because the argument is settled, but because the literature you will read and publish in is overwhelmingly frequentist. You now know a choice was made. Most students never find out. ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Priors (graded) :::: ::::{.task-container} 1. Your assay improves to sensitivity 99%, false positive rate 1%. At 2% prevalence, what does a positive mean now, and is it enough? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} prob_present_given_positive(0.02, sensitivity = 0.99, false_positive_rate = 0.01) ``` ::: 2. Which matters more for a **rare** species: raising sensitivity, or lowering the false positive rate? Use the function, then explain in one sentence. 3. Write `prob_absent_given_negative()`. At 2% prevalence, what does a **negative** mean, and why is that so much more comfortable than the positive case? :::: :::
**1.** About 67%. Better, still not enough to hang a protected-species designation on. Rarity is punishing. **2.** Lowering the false positive rate, by a wide margin, because it operates on the 980 empty ponds while sensitivity operates on only the 20 occupied ones. When the species is rare, almost every chance to be wrong is a chance to be wrong in that direction. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} prob_absent_given_negative <- function(prevalence, sensitivity = 0.90, false_positive_rate = 0.05) { true_negative <- (1 - prevalence) * (1 - false_positive_rate) false_negative <- prevalence * (1 - sensitivity) true_negative / (true_negative + false_negative) } prob_absent_given_negative(0.02) # about 0.998 ``` ::: **3.** A negative is worth about 99.8%: nearly conclusive, where the positive was nearly worthless. Same assay, opposite usefulness, and the asymmetry is entirely the prior. Evidence *for* a rare thing must fight the base rate; evidence *against* it pushes at an open door.
